solution:
All four forces named on the left are electromagnetic in origin. The chapter states that the majority of forces experienced in daily life, such as the force of friction, normal reaction, tension in strings, collision forces, elastic forces and viscosity or fluid friction, are EM in nature.

Tension, the normal force and friction are, in addition, reaction forces. Each of them arises between two surfaces in contact, through a deformation that changes intermolecular distances and thereby produces a reaction: the normal force is the component of that reaction along the common normal, and friction is its parallel or tangential component, while a string becomes taut and pulls back only because it has been stretched. The resistance offered by air or water is not a reaction force in this sense, since it is not developed between two surfaces pressed together; it is the fluid friction that opposes an object moving through the fluid.

Friction and the resistive force of air or water are named in the chapter as non-conservative: the work done against them is strictly path dependent, is not recoverable even if the path is exactly reversed, and appears as heat and sound. Tension is also non-conservative, since no potential energy can be associated with it and the work it does on a body depends on the path followed. The normal force always acts perpendicular to the displacement of the body along the surface, so the work done by it is zero for every path; being trivially path independent it is treated as conservative.

| Name of the force | Type of the force |
|---|---|
| A. Force due to tension in a string | P, Q, S |
| B. Normal force | P, Q, R |
| C. Frictional force | P, Q, S |
| D. Resistive force offered by air or water | P, S |

Thus each of the four is electromagnetic in origin; they differ only in whether they arise as a reaction on contact, and in whether the work done against them can be recovered.
_note: Reviewer note, not a printed defect. The chapter explicitly names friction and air drag as non-conservative, and explicitly calls the normal reaction, friction and tension contact forces that are EM in nature and that arise as reaction forces. It does not itself label tension or the normal force as conservative or non-conservative, so those two cells are a judgement call; the reasoning used is stated in the solution.

solution:
In real life a moving object is never free of opposing forces. There is friction between the surfaces in contact, and there is the viscous drag of the air or of the water through which the object moves. These forces always act opposite to the motion, so even on a horizontal surface there is a resultant unbalanced force on the body.

By Newton's second law this resultant force produces a retardation. The velocity therefore keeps falling and the body eventually comes to rest. This is exactly what Galileo showed while correcting Aristotle's fallacy: a rolling ball stops because of friction, a paper plane because of the viscous force of air, a paper boat because of the viscous force of water.

What is to be done is to apply an external force continuously that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the resultant opposing force, so that the resultant of all the forces on the body becomes zero. With \(\vec{F} = 0\) we get \(\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = 0\), so the velocity does not change and the motion remains uniform.

It should be noted that this does not vindicate Aristotle. The applied force is not needed to maintain the motion; it is needed only to overcome friction and viscous drag. On a perfectly smooth surface in vacuum, no force at all would be required to keep the body moving with uniform velocity.
_note: The book prints the stem as "In real life objects, never travel with uniform velocity..." — the comma belongs after "objects", not after "life" — and it ends this declarative sentence with a question mark. The intended question has been answered.

solution:
Newton's first law is never used directly because it follows from the second law. From \(\vec{F} = m\vec{a}\), if \(\vec{F} = 0\) then \(\vec{a} = 0\), so the velocity does not change; a body at rest stays at rest and a body in uniform motion continues in uniform motion. It must still be studied, because it supplies three ideas that the second law by itself does not.

1. It shows the equivalence between the state of rest and the state of uniform motion along a straight line. Both of them need an external unbalanced force in order to be changed, so both are referred to as a state of motion. The distinction between the two lies only in the choice of the frame of reference.

2. It defines force qualitatively, as an entity or physical quantity that brings about a change in the state of motion of a body, that is, something that initiates or controls a motion. The second law only gives the quantitative measure, or the mathematical expression, of a force that has already been defined in this way.

3. It defines inertia as a fundamental property of every physical object, by which the object resists any change in its state of motion. Inertia is measured as the mass of the object, more specifically the inertial mass, \(m = \frac{|\vec{F}|}{|\vec{a}|}\).

Besides these, the first law is the test by which a frame of reference is classified: any frame of reference in which Newton's first law of motion is applicable is an inertial frame of reference, and one in which a body suffers an acceleration in the absence of a net force is a non-inertial frame.

Thus the first law is the conceptual foundation on which the other two laws rest, and it must be studied even though it is not applied directly.

Yes, there are such situations. Newton's laws of motion cannot be applied in the following cases.

1. In a non-inertial frame of reference, that is, a frame having an acceleration. Newton's laws are applicable only in inertial frames.

2. For objects that cannot be treated as point objects, and for bodies that are not rigid. The laws are stated for point objects, and they hold for rigid bodies, in which the relative distances between the particles do not change under any deforming force.

3. For objects moving with speeds comparable to that of light. Newton's laws then do not give results that match the experimental results.

4. For the behaviour and interaction of objects having atomic or molecular sizes.

There is an alternative in each case.

1. If the frame of reference has an acceleration \(\vec{a}\), a pseudo force \(-m\vec{a}\) is included along with all the other forces while writing the force equations. Newton's laws can then be used within that accelerated frame itself.

2. A finite object is replaced by a point object situated at its centre of mass, at which the entire mass of the body may be assumed to be concentrated. This is precisely why the concept of the centre of mass is introduced.

3. For speeds comparable to that of light, Einstein's special theory of relativity has to be used.

4. At the atomic and molecular level, quantum mechanics has to be used.

You are pushed towards your right whenever your own frame of reference, the capsule, has an acceleration towards your left. This happens if the capsule suddenly starts moving towards your left, or if it is moving towards your right and is being braked, or if it takes a turn towards the left, when the centripetal acceleration is directed to the left. In every one of these cases the capsule is an accelerated, that is a non-inertial, frame of reference, and the force you experience is a pseudo force. Its magnitude is \(ma\), where \(m\) is your mass and \(\vec{a}\) is the acceleration of the capsule, and it is written as \(-m\vec{a}\), the negative sign showing that its direction is opposite to that of the acceleration of the frame.

It is not merely a feeling; it is a reality in the sense that it is measurable. If you were standing on a weighing scale, or if a force measuring device were suitably placed, the force would actually be recorded. The word pseudo does not mean imaginary; it means non-real, and the force is called non-real only because it is not among the four fundamental forces and cannot be accounted for by Newton's second law in an inertial frame.

One more situation of the same kind is standing inside a bus. When the bus starts to move you are pushed backwards, when it is about to stop you are pushed forwards, and when it takes a turn you are pushed towards the outer side. Similarly, inside a lift that has just started moving up you feel heavier, and a weighing scale actually records an increased weight \(W = mg + ma\); while the lift undergoes downward acceleration in order to stop at an upper floor you feel lighter, and the scale records \(W = mg - ma\).

The one force that governs daily life almost entirely is the electromagnetic force.

The two nuclear forces are ruled out by their range. The strong nuclear force, though the strongest of all, is a short range force acting over less than \(10^{-14}\) m, and the range of the weak nuclear force is smaller still, of the order of \(10^{-16}\) m. Neither of them operates over the distances we deal with; they act only inside a nucleus, and are responsible for binding the nucleons and for radioactive decay.

The gravitational force reaches us in daily life only as our weight, the pull of the Earth, \(W = \frac{GMm}{R^2} = mg\). Between ordinary objects around us it is negligibly small. For two SUMO wrestlers of mass 300 kg each, only 0.5 m apart,
\(F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 300\times 300}{0.5^2} \cong 24\times 10^{-5}\ \text{N} = 24\ \mu\text{N}\),
against a weight of about 3000 N for each of them.

Everything else that we actually experience is electromagnetic in nature: the friction that lets us walk and hold things, the normal reaction of the floor and of a chair, the tension in strings and ropes, elastic forces, the forces during collisions, viscosity and air drag, and all chemical and biological processes in and around us. Hence the statement is justified: the electromagnetic force governs our daily life almost entirely.

Consider the three one by one. The force responsible for a string becoming taut on stretching is the tension in the string. The force due to which we can hold an object in the hand is the friction between the hand and the object, together with the normal reaction. Both of these are contact forces: they act only on contact, arise from a deformation that changes intermolecular distances, and are electromagnetic in nature.

The weight of an object is the gravitational force exerted on it by the Earth, \(W = mg\). It is a non-contact force, and it is gravitational and not electromagnetic in origin.

Hence the odd man out is the weight of an object.

Yes. Every pair of masses attracts each other, so there is a gravitational force of attraction between the two of us, given by \(F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\).

We do not come together because this force is negligibly small. The chapter's illustration makes the size of it clear. For two SUMO wrestlers of mass 300 kg each, sitting only 0.5 m apart,
\(F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 300\times 300}{0.5^2} \cong 24\ \mu\text{N}\),
while the weight of each of them is about 3000 N. For two ordinary persons the mutual attraction is smaller still, being of the order of a few micronewtons, which is far too feeble to set either of us into motion.

Yes, forces other than the gravitational force of the Earth do come into the picture. Sitting on the ground we experience the normal reaction given by the ground, which balances our weight, and any tendency to slide towards each other is opposed by the force of friction between us and the ground. Both of these are contact forces and are electromagnetic in nature, and each of them is enormously larger than the mutual gravitational attraction. That is why the tiny gravitational pull between us never produces any observable motion.

Real and pseudo forces:

| Real force | Pseudo force |
|---|---|
| It is one of the four fundamental forces in nature. | It is not among any of the four fundamental forces. |
| It arises from a genuine interaction between two bodies, so there is always an equal and opposite reaction force on the other body. | It arises only because the frame of reference itself is accelerated; no other body exerts it, so it has no reaction force. |
| It obeys Newton's laws of motion and is accountable in an inertial frame of reference. | It is not accountable as per Newton's second law in an inertial frame of reference. |
| It exists in every frame of reference. | It appears only in a non-inertial frame; it is measured to be \(-m\vec{a}\), directed opposite to the acceleration \(\vec{a}\) of the frame. |

Both are measurable with instruments, so a pseudo force is non-real, not imaginary.

Conservative and non-conservative forces:

| Conservative force | Non-conservative force |
|---|---|
| The work done by or against it is independent of the actual path, and depends only upon the initial and final positions. | The work done against it is strictly path dependent. |
| The work done in a complete round trip is zero, and the work done is recoverable. | The work done is not recoverable even if the path is exactly reversed. |
| A potential energy can be defined for it, \(dU = -\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{x}\), and the mechanical energy is conserved. | No potential energy can be defined; the work done against it appears as heat, sound, light, etc. |
| Examples: gravitational force, elastic force of a spring. | Examples: force of friction, air drag, viscous force. |

Contact and non-contact forces:

| Contact force | Non-contact force |
|---|---|
| Physical contact between the objects is an essential condition. | Physical contact is not essential; the force exists even if the objects are distant or physically separated. |
| It results from a deformation that changes intermolecular distances, and therefore appears as a reaction force. | No deformation is involved. |
| All contact forces are electromagnetic in nature. | They may be gravitational, electrostatic, magnetostatic, and so on. |
| Examples: normal reaction, force of friction, tension in a string, forces occurring during a collision. | Examples: gravitational force between the Earth and the moon, force between two magnets, electrostatic force between charges. |

Inertial and non-inertial frames of reference:

| Inertial frame of reference | Non-inertial frame of reference |
|---|---|
| Newton's first law of motion is applicable in it. | Newton's first law of motion is not applicable in it. |
| The frame itself is unaccelerated. | The frame itself has an acceleration. |
| If there is no net force, a body moves with a constant velocity, which may be zero; if there is no net force there is no acceleration. | In the absence of a net force, an object is still found to suffer an acceleration. |
| No pseudo force is needed, and Newton's laws can be applied directly. | A pseudo force \(-m\vec{a}\) must be added to all the other forces before Newton's laws can be used. |
| Examples: a rocket in intergalactic space with all its engines shut; for any day-to-day situation, a frame attached to the Earth. | Examples: a car that is just starting or is being braked, a lift while accelerating, a merry-go-round. |
_note: The book labels the four sub-parts (A), (B), (C), (C); the fourth should read (D). All four distinctions have been answered.

solution:
The popular formula for calculating the work done by a force is
\(W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s} = F s \cos\theta\),
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the applied force \(\vec{F}\) and the displacement \(\vec{s}\).

Yes, there is a limitation. This formula is applicable only if both the force \(\vec{F}\) and the displacement \(\vec{s}\) are constant and finite. In several real life situations the force is not constant. While lifting an object through several thousand kilometres the gravitational force is not constant, and viscous forces such as fluid resistance depend upon the speed and hence are quite often not constant with time. For such a variable force the product \(F s \cos\theta\) has no meaning and cannot be used directly.

There is a mathematical way out, and it is integration. The displacement is divided into a very large number of infinitesimal displacements. One such displacement \(ds\) is taken to be so small that the force \(F\) is practically constant over it, meaning that the change in the force over it is too small to be recorded. The work done over this displacement is then
\(dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s}\),
and the total work done for a displacement from \(s_1\) to \(s_2\) is obtained by adding up all such contributions, that is, by integration:
\(W = \int_{s_1}^{s_2} F\,ds\).

This method of integration is applicable provided the exact way in which \(\vec{F}\) varies with \(\vec{s}\) is known and that function is integrable. Graphically the same quantity is the area under the force-displacement curve between \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), which is valid only if the force axis necessarily starts from zero.

Work and energy are measured in the same unit, the joule, and have the same dimensions. Neither of them is ever met with independently of the other, and each is continually converted into the other. That is why they are described as two sides of one coin.

Energy is defined as the capacity to do work: a body possesses energy exactly in the measure of the work it is able to perform. Conversely, work done on a body does not disappear, it appears as energy of the body.

The work-energy theorem states this quantitatively: the change in the kinetic energy of a body is equal to the work done by the force. For a body of mass \(m\) slowed from \(u\) to \(v\) by a constant opposing force \(F\) acting over a displacement \(s\),
\(\frac{1}{2}mu^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = F s\),
the left hand side being the decrease in the kinetic energy and the right hand side the work done by that force. When work is done against a conservative force, an equal amount of potential energy is stored in the body, \(dU = -\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{x}\), and when the body later moves under that force the stored potential energy is converted back into kinetic energy. When work is done against a non-conservative force such as friction, it is again not lost but appears as heat, sound or light.

Thus work is the process by which energy is transferred or transformed from one form to another, and energy is the quantity that is so transferred. One cannot be described without the other, which justifies the statement that work and energy are the two sides of a coin.

No, the relation is not applicable exactly. The ball falls through air, so besides the conservative gravitational force there is a non-conservative resistive force, the air resistance, acting upon it. While coming down, the potential energy of the ball decreases and an equal amount of work is done, but this work is not entirely converted into kinetic energy; a part of it is used up in overcoming the air resistance and appears in other forms such as heat and sound. The work-energy theorem in this case is written as
\(\Delta \text{P.E.} = \Delta \text{K.E.} + W_{\text{air resistance}}\),
that is,
\(mgH = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + W_{\text{air resistance}}\).
Hence \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 < mgH\).

The difference is accounted for by the work done against the air resistance. The magnitude of the resistive force is not constant but depends upon the speed of the ball, so this work has to be evaluated as the work done against a variable force,
\(W_{\text{air resistance}} = \int \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s}\).
The relation \(mgH = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) would be exact only if the ball fell in vacuum.

No, the ball will not bounce back to the same height from where it was dropped. The collision of the ball with the ground is an inelastic collision, so kinetic energy is lost during the impact itself, being spent in deforming the ball and reappearing as heat and sound; and air resistance acts on the ball once again while it rises. The ball therefore rebounds to a smaller height. It would return exactly to the same height only if the collision were perfectly elastic and the whole event took place in an evacuated space.

[Textbook misprint: the stem reads "Given an example from our daily life" where the imperative "Give" belongs.]

Law of conservation of linear momentum: the total momentum of an isolated system is conserved during any interaction. Here an isolated system means one on which there is no external force, and an interaction refers to a collision, an explosion, and so on.

It is a consequence of Newton's second law of motion. According to the second law the resultant force is equal to the rate of change of linear momentum, \(\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}\). Hence if \(\vec{F} = 0\), then \(\frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = 0\) and \(\vec{p}\) is constant, that is, the linear momentum is conserved. Newton's third law completes the picture for the members of the system, because the mutual forces they exert on one another during the interaction are equal and opposite and are internal forces for the system as a whole.

An example from daily life is the recoil of a gun. Before firing, the gun and the bullet are at rest, so the total momentum of the system is zero. On firing, the bullet of mass \(m\) moves forward with velocity \(\vec{v}\), and the gun of mass \(M\) must therefore move backward with a velocity \(\vec{V}\) such that \(m\vec{v} + M\vec{V} = 0\). This backward motion of the gun is the recoil. The backward thrust felt while holding a hose pipe ejecting water, and the propulsion of a rocket, are examples of the same kind.

Yes, it holds good during the burst of a cracker. The forces developed during the explosion act between the fragments of the cracker themselves, so they are internal forces for the system consisting of all the fragments. In the absence of an external force, the vector sum of the momenta of all the fragments immediately after the burst is therefore exactly equal to the momentum of the cracker just before it burst. It may be noted that the kinetic energy is not conserved during an explosion, since energy is supplied internally and the final kinetic energy is greater than the initial, but the total linear momentum is conserved.
_note: The book prints "Given an example from our daily life"; "Give an example" is meant.

solution:
For a collision between two objects, the negative of the ratio of the relative velocity of separation to the relative velocity of approach is defined as the coefficient of restitution \(e\).

Consider a head-on collision of two bodies of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), with initial velocities \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) and final velocities \(v_1\) and \(v_2\). The relative velocity of approach is \(u_a = u_2 - u_1\) and the relative velocity of separation is \(v_s = v_2 - v_1\). Hence
\(e = -\frac{v_s}{u_a} = -\frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_2 - u_1} = \frac{v_1 - v_2}{u_2 - u_1} = \frac{\text{relative speed of separation}}{\text{relative speed of approach}}\).

Value for an elastic collision: for such a collision both the linear momentum and the total kinetic energy of the system are conserved. Conservation of momentum gives
\(m_1(u_1 - v_1) = m_2(v_2 - u_2)\),
and conservation of kinetic energy gives
\(m_1(u_1 + v_1)(u_1 - v_1) = m_2(u_2 + v_2)(v_2 - u_2)\).
Dividing the second by the first,
\(u_1 + v_1 = u_2 + v_2 \quad \therefore u_2 - u_1 = v_1 - v_2\).
Substituting this in the definition,
\(e = \frac{v_1 - v_2}{u_2 - u_1} = 1\).

Value for a perfectly inelastic collision: here the colliding bodies join together and move jointly after the collision, so their final velocities are the same, \(v_2 = v_1\), giving \(v_2 - v_1 = 0\). Hence
\(e = 0\).

Thus \(e = 1\) for an elastic collision and \(e = 0\) for a perfectly inelastic collision, and for any collision the coefficient of restitution lies between 0 and 1.

[Textbook misprint: the stem reads "A veru heavy object" for "A very heavy object". The next sub-item spells it correctly.]

For a head-on elastic collision of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) having initial velocities \(u_1\) and \(u_2\), the final velocities are
\(v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_1 + \left(\frac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_2\)
and
\(v_2 = \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_2 + \left(\frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_1\).

(i) Colliding bodies are identical. Here \(m_1 = m_2 = m\), so that \(m_1 - m_2 = 0\) and \(\frac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2} = 1\). The two expressions reduce to
\(v_1 = u_2\) and \(v_2 = u_1\).
Thus the two bodies just exchange their velocities. These results are exact.

(ii) A very heavy object collides on a lighter object, initially at rest. Here \(m_1 \gg m_2\) and \(u_2 = 0\), so we may use the approximations \(m_1 \pm m_2 \cong m_1\) and \(\frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2} \cong 0\). The expressions then give
\(v_1 \cong u_1\) and \(v_2 \cong 2u_1\).
Thus the massive striking body is practically unaffected, and the tiny body which is struck travels with double the speed of the massive striking body. These results are approximate.

(iii) A very light object collides on a comparatively much massive object, initially at rest. Here \(m_1 \ll m_2\) and \(u_2 = 0\). Using similar approximations,
\(v_1 \cong -u_1\) and \(v_2 \cong 0\).
Thus the tiny or lighter object rebounds with the same speed in exactly the opposite direction, while the massive object remains unaffected. This is as good as dropping an elastic object on the hard surface of the Earth. These results are also approximate.
_note: The book prints "A veru heavy object" in sub-part (ii); "very" is meant.

solution:
The bullet gets embedded into the block, so the two move jointly after the impact. This is therefore a perfectly inelastic, head-on collision, with \(u_1 = u\) and \(u_2 = 0\). Let \(v\) be their common velocity after the collision.

By the principle of conservation of linear momentum,
\(m_1 u + m_2(0) = (m_1 + m_2)v \quad \therefore v = \frac{m_1 u}{m_1 + m_2}\).

Loss in kinetic energy of the system,
\(\Delta(\text{K.E.}) = \frac{1}{2}m_1u^2 - \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)v^2\)
\(= \frac{1}{2}m_1u^2 - \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)\left(\frac{m_1u}{m_1 + m_2}\right)^2\)
\(= \frac{1}{2}m_1u^2 - \frac{1}{2}\frac{m_1^2u^2}{m_1 + m_2}\)
\(= \frac{1}{2}m_1u^2\left(1 - \frac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)\)
\(\therefore \Delta(\text{K.E.}) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u^2\).

The masses and \(u^2\) are always positive, so there is always a loss of kinetic energy, and since the collision is perfectly inelastic this loss is the maximum possible.

No, this does not violate the principle of conservation of energy. What is lost is only the kinetic energy of the system, not its total energy. While the bullet ploughs into the wood, the lost kinetic energy is spent in permanently deforming the block and the bullet and in overcoming the internal friction between them, and it reappears as heat, as sound and as vibrational energy of the atoms of the two bodies, which is why the block and the bullet are perceptibly warmer after the impact. When all these forms are added, the total energy of the system after the collision is exactly equal to that before it.

The quantity related to the change in momentum is the impulse of the force, \(\vec{J}\). It is defined as the change in momentum produced by the force,
\(\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = \vec{p}_2 - \vec{p}_1\).

According to Newton's second law \(\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}\), so that \(d\vec{p} = \vec{F}\,dt\). If the force is constant and acts for a finite and measurable time \(t\), the change in momentum in that time is
\(\vec{J} = \vec{p}_2 - \vec{p}_1 = m(\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1) = \vec{F}t\).

For a variable force the product \(\vec{F}t\) has no meaning, since there is no single value of \(\vec{F}\). If we know how the force varies with time, the impulse must be obtained by integrating over the interval for which the force acts:
\(\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = \int d\vec{p} = \int \vec{F}\,dt\).
Graphically this is the area under the force-time curve for that interval, the force axis necessarily starting from zero. Generally the force is zero before the impact, rises to a maximum and falls to zero after it. This is also why a wicket keeper draws his hands back while catching a fast ball: the area under the curve, and hence the impulse, is fixed by the change in momentum of the ball, so by increasing the time of collision he reduces the maximum force he has to withstand.

We define impulse instead of using the force whenever an appreciable force acts for an extremely small interval of time, too small for the force and the time to be measured independently. Hitting a ball with a bat, giving a kick to a football, hammering a nail and bouncing a ball from a hard surface are all of this kind. In such cases the force itself is not easily recordable, but its effect, the change in momentum of the object, is noticeable and can be measured; so it is convenient to define the change in momentum itself as a physical quantity.

The process is easy for us when the applied force is large, when it is applied at a point as far as possible from the axis of rotation, and when it is applied along a direction perpendicular to the line joining the axis of rotation with the point of application.

The reason lies in the expression for the rotational effect of a force. Its magnitude is
\(\tau = rF\sin\theta\),
where \(r\) is the distance of the point of application from the axis of rotation and \(\theta\) is the smaller angle between the directions of \(\vec{r}\) and \(\vec{F}\). Hence if \(r\) or \(F\) is greater, the rotational effect is greater, which is why the handle of a door is fixed away from the hinges and why a heavier door needs a proportionally larger force. If \(\theta = 90^\circ\), then \(\tau = \tau_{\max} = rF\), so the force should be applied along the normal direction for easy rotation. If \(\theta = 0^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\), then \(\tau = 0\), so a force applied parallel or antiparallel to \(\vec{r}\), that is nearly along the door, produces no rotation at all.

The vector quantity concerned is the moment of a force, also called torque. It is the rotational analogue of a force, and in its mathematical form it is given by
\(\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}\),
where \(\vec{F}\) is the applied force and \(\vec{r}\) is the position vector of the point of application of the force from the axis of rotation. Its direction is always perpendicular to the plane containing \(\vec{r}\) and \(\vec{F}\), and is obtained by the rule of the cross product or by the right-hand thumb rule.

A pair of two forces of equal magnitude acting in opposite directions along different lines of action is called a couple, and its rotational effect is the moment of the couple. The two cases differ as follows.

| Moment of a force | Moment of a couple |
|---|---|
| \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}\) | \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}_{12}\times\vec{F}_1 = \vec{r}_{21}\times\vec{F}_2\) |
| It depends upon the axis of rotation and upon the point of application of the force, so the same force can have different torques for different points of application. | It depends only upon the two forces, that is, it is independent of the axis of rotation and of the points of application of the forces. |
| It can produce a translational acceleration also, if the axis of rotation is not fixed or if friction is not enough. | It does not produce any translational acceleration, but produces only rotational or angular acceleration. |

A couple consists of two forces of equal magnitude \(F\) acting in opposite directions along two different lines of action, separated by a perpendicular distance \(r\). Because the two forces are equal and opposite, their individual moments about any axis combine into a quantity that contains only \(F\) and the separation \(r\), and every distance that fixes the position of the axis cancels out. This is seen by taking the two possible positions of a fixed axis of rotation for the same couple acting on the same object.

Case 1: the axis of rotation lies between the lines of action of the two forces. Let the perpendicular distances of the axis from the forces \(\vec{F}\) and \(-\vec{F}\) be \(x\) and \(y\) respectively. In this case the rotation due to both the forces is in the same sense, so the two individual torques are directed the same way and add up:
\(\tau = \tau_+ + \tau_- = xF + yF = (x + y)F = rF\).

Case 2: the lines of action of both the forces are on the same side of the axis of rotation, at perpendicular distances \(q\) and \(p\) from it. Now one of the forces tends to rotate the body anticlockwise and the other clockwise, so the individual torques are oppositely directed and subtract:
\(\tau = \tau_+ - \tau_- = qF - pF = (q - p)F = rF\).

In both cases the result is the same, \(\tau = rF\), and it contains no quantity that locates the axis. The same conclusion follows from the vector form, \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}_{12}\times\vec{F}_1 = \vec{r}_{21}\times\vec{F}_2\); since \(r_{12}\sin\alpha = r_{21}\sin\beta = r\), the magnitude is \(\tau = r_{12}F_1\sin\alpha = r_{21}F_2\sin\beta = rF\), whichever point on either line of action is chosen.

Hence the moment of a given couple is constant. It depends only upon the magnitude of either force and upon the separation between their lines of action, and is therefore independent of the position of the axis of rotation even when that axis is fixed. This is unlike the moment of a single force, for which a reaction force appears at the fixed axis and the torque changes with the point of application of the force.

Balancing, or mechanical equilibrium, is a consequence of Newton's second law of motion. According to that law the momentum of a system is constant in the absence of an external unbalanced force, and this state is called mechanical equilibrium.

A particle is said to be in mechanical equilibrium if no net force is acting upon it. For a system of bodies the condition is stricter: the net force acting on any part of the system should be zero. In other words, the velocity or the linear momentum of all the parts of the system must be constant, or zero, and there must be no acceleration in any part of the system. Mathematically,
\(\sum\vec{F} = 0\)
for every part of the system.

A rotating fan is not in mechanical equilibrium. It is true that the fan as a whole does not move from its place, so the linear velocity of the fan taken as a whole, that is the velocity of its centre of mass, is zero. But mechanical equilibrium requires the condition to be satisfied by every part of the system, and here it is not. Each small part of a rotating blade moves along a circle, so its velocity is continuously changing in direction. It therefore possesses a centripetal acceleration directed towards the axis of rotation, and a non-zero net force must be acting upon it to provide that acceleration.

Since there is an acceleration, and hence a non-zero resultant force, in parts of the system, the rotating fan is not in mechanical equilibrium even though its linear velocity as a whole is zero.

Newton's laws of motion, and many other laws, are stated for point masses only. In real life we always come across finite objects, that is, objects of measurable size. The concept of the centre of mass helps us to consider such an object to be a point object situated at a particular location, at which the entire mass of the body may be assumed to be concentrated, and thereby allows us to apply Newton's laws of motion to it. In this sense the centre of mass is the particle equivalent of a given object.

Knowing it is useful in other ways as well. It is the point at which, if a force is applied, the force causes only a linear acceleration and no angular acceleration; correspondingly, if the line of action of a force passes through it, the moment of that force is zero. Its location can be changed only by an external unbalanced force, so internal forces, such as those acting during a collision or an explosion, never change it. For a system of only two particles it divides the distance between them in the inverse ratio of their masses, and for a body having an axis of symmetry it lies on that axis, or at the point of intersection if there are several such axes. It is also the point about which the summation of the moments of the masses of the system is zero.

The centre of gravity of a body is the point around which the resultant torque due to the force of gravity on the body is zero; analogous to the centre of mass, it is the weighted average of the gravitational forces, that is the weights, on the individual particles. For a uniform gravitational field, in simple words if \(g\) is constant over the body, the centre of gravity always coincides with the centre of mass. This is true for all the objects on the Earth that we meet in daily life, which is why in common usage the two terms are used for the same purpose.

The position of the centre of mass may therefore differ from that of the centre of gravity only for an object over which the gravitational field is appreciably non-uniform. On the Earth this is possible only if the size of the object is comparable to that of the Earth itself, that is, at least a few thousand kilometres. For such an object the gravitational field is stronger on its lower side, so its centre of gravity lies slightly lower than its centre of mass, and the centre of gravity also depends upon the orientation of the object, whereas the centre of mass is a fixed property of a given rigid body irrespective of its orientation. In practice we shall not come across such an object.
